explanations.answer: Among the upright in the assembly
explanations.explanation: That's the spot, baker. He says it plainly: "in the council of the upright and in the assembly." He isn't saving his thanks for a quiet corner where nobody can hear him. I think a man that thankful wants company.

A cave does give you a great echo, I'll say that. But the psalmist never mentions a cave. He says he'll give thanks "in the council of the upright and in the assembly." That's a room full of people, not a room full of rocks.

A riverbank sounds peaceful, friend, but this psalm doesn't say a word about water. He plans to give thanks "in the council of the upright and in the assembly." With all his heart and a crowd around him, he doesn't need a view.

Pondered is the word, baker. The folks who delight in the LORD's works turn them over and think them through. That's slow, happy thinking. I do the same thing with a tray of cookies cooling on the rack, except I get distracted and eat one.

Counting is quick, friend. You hit the last number and you're done. The verse says the works are pondered by those who delight in them, and that's more like sitting with something and letting it sink in.

Guarding sounds serious, like somebody standing at the door with crossed arms. But the verse doesn't post any guards. It says the works are pondered by all who delight in them. These people aren't protecting the works, they're enjoying them.

Forever, baker! The psalmist says it flat out: "His righteousness endures forever." No end date, no fine print. And he isn't done with that word. He uses it again in the very same psalm, and we'll hear it more.
One lifetime is a long time to us, friend, but the psalm goes bigger. It says His righteousness "endures forever." That's way past one lifetime. It never stops.
Kings come and go, baker. A new one takes over and everything changes. But the psalmist puts no handoff date on God's righteousness. He says it "endures forever."

True, baker. Right there in the verse: "He has caused His wonders to be remembered…" He's the one who makes sure they don't get lost. Then the psalmist adds that the LORD is gracious and compassionate.

This one is actually true, friend. The psalmist says, "He has caused His wonders to be remembered…" So the LORD Himself makes sure His wonders are remembered. Easy one to doubt, but the verse is clear.

Covenant is it, baker. The LORD provides food for those who fear Him, and He remembers His covenant forever. That word "forever" keeps showing up in this psalm. Some of us can't remember where we put our oven mitts, and He remembers His covenant forever.
A temple is a fine thing, friend, but this verse doesn't mention one. It says the LORD "remembers His covenant forever." The psalmist is talking about what God promised, not a building.

A throne sounds grand, baker, but the verse doesn't go there. It says He provides food for those who fear Him and remembers His covenant forever. That's a promise He keeps in mind, not a piece of furniture.

explanations.answer: By giving them the inheritance of the nations
explanations.explanation: That's what the psalmist says, baker. The LORD showed His people the power of His works "by giving them the inheritance of the nations." It wasn't a rumor, it was something they could see. When someone hands you an inheritance, you don't need a lecture on how strong He is.

explanations.answer: By raising their king above all the nations
explanations.explanation: That sounds impressive, friend, but the psalmist doesn't say it. He says the LORD showed His people the power of His works by giving them the inheritance of the nations. No king gets mentioned in this verse.

explanations.answer: By sending fire upon all of their enemies
explanations.explanation: Fire makes for a dramatic answer, baker, but it isn't in this psalm. The psalmist says the LORD showed the power of His works by giving His people the inheritance of the nations. Nothing about fire or enemies here.
Trustworthy, baker! The psalmist says, "all His precepts are trustworthy." You can lean your whole weight on them. In a world where I can't even trust a timer to ring, that's good news.
Temporary is the opposite of what he says, friend. The next verse says they're "upheld forever and ever." So the precepts are trustworthy, and they last.
I get it, baker, sometimes the Bible feels like a big recipe with a lot of steps. But the psalmist doesn't say complicated. He says all His precepts are trustworthy, and that's the word to hang onto.
Redemption, baker! The psalmist says, "He has sent redemption to His people." That's the best news in the psalm. It's something He sent, not something they had to go fetch.
Judgment isn't the word in this verse, friend. The psalmist says the LORD "has sent redemption to His people." That's the good news he's celebrating.
Famine goes the opposite direction, baker. Back in verse 5 the psalmist says the LORD provides food for those who fear Him. Here, what He sends to His people is redemption.

Holy and awesome, baker. The psalmist says it right at the end of verse 9: "holy and awesome is His name." After talking about everything the LORD has done, he stops to honor who He is. Nothing more to add to that one.

explanations.answer: It is hidden from the nations
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this psalm says His name is hidden, friend. The psalmist says, "holy and awesome is His name." He's talking about how great the name is, not who gets to hear it.

explanations.answer: It is spoken only by priests
explanations.explanation: The psalm doesn't say that, baker. It never mentions priests at all. The psalmist simply says, "holy and awesome is His name."

That's the starting line, baker. The psalmist says, "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom…" It's where wisdom begins, before everything else. And the more you know me, the more you'll see I started at the beginning of every recipe too, mostly.

Study is a good thing, friend, but the psalmist doesn't say wisdom starts there. He says, "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom…" Wisdom starts with the LORD, not with the length of your reading list.
Good advice from folks who've lived a while is nice to have, baker. But that isn't what the psalmist names. He says, "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom…" That's where it all starts.
True, baker! The psalmist says, "all who follow His precepts gain rich understanding." Follow them, and the understanding comes. And the psalm ends the way it began, with praise.
This one is true, friend. The psalmist says, "all who follow His precepts gain rich understanding." That's a promise for everyone who follows, with no catch in the verse.
